channel.title: field/notes by Timothy Castillon
channel.description: A field record of the people and places carrying the weight of a changing world: labor, land, and the communities closest to both, documented up close and credited where I can.

item.title: Angkor: Stone, Water, and the Labor of Upkeep
item.description:
ANGKOR ARCHAEOLOGICAL PARK, SIEM REAP, KH, NOV 2026

In Angkor, the temples don't sit apart from the land. They're held up by water and constant human presence.

item.title: Zion: The Grandeur of Verticality
item.description:
ZION NATIONAL PARK, UT, SEP 2026

In Zion, the canyon walls pull your eyes straight up, but what stuck with me happened down along the Virgin River. Walking the trail with my uncle, the sheer cliffs of Navajo sandstone felt untouchable, until you realize the quiet itself had to be engineered.

item.title: Valley of Fire: The Aesthetics of Aridity
item.description:
VALLEY OF FIRE, NV, APR 2026

In the Mojave, the land doesn't hide how fragile it is. I spent the afternoon out here with my uncle, and at one point he pointed at the red Aztec sandstone and said it looked scorched, like the sun had been sitting on it too long.

item.title: Atok: The Salad Bowl Above the Clouds
item.description:
ATOK, BENGUET, PH, JAN 2026

In Atok, the mountain ridges aren't just scenery. They're carved into neat green rows that end up on Manila's tables.

item.title: Merkato: The Hide Trade of Addis Ababa
item.description:
ADDIS ABABA, ET, NOV 2025

Merkato runs on hands most of the city never sees up close. People call it the largest open-air market in Africa, and its hide sellers are out there from early morning, stretching raw skins, sorting them by grade, and folding them into rust-orange stacks that end up as shoes and bags an ocean away.

item.title: Crete: Stone, Salt, and Summer Light
item.description:
CHANIA, GEORGIOUPOLI, LAKE KOURNAS & TRIOPETRA, CRETE, GR, JUL 2025

In Crete, everything sits right where dry rock meets open water. Moving between the Venetian harbor in Chania, the stone causeway out to the whitewashed chapel in Georgioupoli, and the layered sea cliffs at Triopetra, you feel how tightly life on the island hugs the shoreline.

item.title: Islas Ballestas: The Poor Man's Galápagos
item.description:
ISLAS BALLESTAS, PE, JUN 2025

Islas Ballestas is built on what nests there: sea lions, Humboldt penguins, and dense colonies of seabirds whose droppings once drove Peru's 19th-century guano boom before the islands became a marine reserve. Now the boats run on tourism instead, steered by local captains whose income rises and falls with an ocean they have no control over.

item.title: Vinicunca: Life on the Rainbow Mountain
item.description:
VINICUNCA, PE, MAR 2025

Everyone comes to Vinicunca for the colors, but the local families working the trail are the ones actually keeping the mountain running. They bring their own horses and alpacas, walking the steep climb on foot beside paying tourists through weather that flips from clear sky to thick fog in under an hour, in air thin enough to leave you winded just from talking.

item.title: Cabrillo: Cliffs at the Edge of the Harbor
item.description:
POINT LOMA, SAN DIEGO, CA, US, OCT 2024

On the tip of Point Loma, two completely different coastlines sit back to back. Look east from the ridge and you see San Diego Bay packed with naval ships, runways, and concrete piers.

item.title: New York City: Concrete, Harbor, and Unpredictable Skies
item.description:
NEW YORK CITY, NY, US, APR 2024

In New York City, tourism never really stops for the weather, even when the sky turns sideways. Visiting in April 2024, one day opened clear over Times Square and the stone facade of the Met, and the next dropped cold rain and sleet across the harbor.

item.title: Grindelwald: The Architecture of Instability
item.description:
GRINDELWALD, CH, MAR 2024

From the town below in Grindelwald, peaks like the Eiger and Wetterhorn look permanent, carved out of solid rock and ice. Up on the slopes, the mountain is loosening its grip.

item.title: Lavaux: The Mirror of Lake Geneva
item.description:
SAINT-SAPHORIN & CHEXBRES, CH, MAY 2023

In Lavaux, the land doesn't just hold the vineyards. It cradles them on steep stone terraces built by hand over centuries.

item.title: Bethlehem & the Judean Hills: Stone, Faith, and Quiet
item.description:
BETHLEHEM & JERUSALEM, WEST BANK, JAN 2023

Looking up inside the dome at the Chapel of the Shepherds' Field in Beit Sahour, with light filtering through the ceiling above the nativity frescoes, there is a stillness that stays with you long after you step back out into the bright limestone streets. Outside, the city spreads across pale terraced hillsides before dropping abruptly into the dry, bare folds of the Judean Desert, where flags snap against utility poles in the wind.

item.title: Nice: Coastline at Low Tide
item.description:
NICE, FR, OCT 2022

This one sits apart from the rest of the journal: a personal trip along the Côte d'Azur, not a documentary assignment, and I'd rather say that upfront than dress it up. Pastel shutters and centuries-old facades share a block with the modern city without much friction.

item.title: Berat: Stone Walls and Sidewalk Looms
item.description:
BERAT, AL, AUG 2022

In Berat, daily trade happens right on the stone walls of the old town. Walking up through the steep cobblestone lanes toward the citadel, you pass hand-knitted wool socks and vests hung on arched doorways, embroidered dresses clipped to wire lines, and woven kilim rugs draped straight over limestone masonry.

item.title: Mombasa: Tides, Reefs, and the Beach Economy
item.description:
BAMBURI, NYALI & MOMBASA, KE, APR 2022

Along the coast in Mombasa, the beach is both a resort backdrop and a crowded workplace. Walk down to the water at low tide and the whole informal economy is laid out in plain sight: handlers leading camels across the white sand for tourist photos, boat crews waiting beside glass-bottom reef cruisers, and local fishermen hauling wooden canoes through the shallows by hand.
